title: Child Nicotine Poisoning Prevention Act of 2015
official_summary:
(This measure has not been amended since it was passed by the Senate on December 10, 2015. The summary of that version is repeated here.)

Child Nicotine Poisoning Prevention Act of 2015

(Sec. 2) This bill requires any nicotine provided in a liquid nicotine container sold, offered for sale, manufactured for sale, distributed in commerce, or imported into the United States to be packaged in accordance with the Consumer Product Safety Commission's (CPSC's) standards and testing procedures for special packaging that is difficult for children under five years of age to open or to obtain harmful contents from. The requirement must be treated as a standard for the special packaging of a household substance under the Poison Prevention Packaging Act of 1970.

"Liquid nicotine container" is defined to: (1) include a package from which nicotine in a solution or other form is accessible through normal and foreseeable use by a consumer and that is used to hold soluble nicotine in any concentration; and (2) exclude a sealed, pre-filled, and disposable container of nicotine in a solution or other form in which such container is inserted directly into an electronic cigarette, electronic nicotine delivery system, or other similar product, if the nicotine in the container is inaccessible through customary or reasonably foreseeable handling or use, including reasonably foreseeable ingestion or other contact by children.

The bill applies to any form of chemical nicotine, including any salt or complex, regardless of whether the chemical is naturally or synthetically derived.

The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) must consult with the CPSC if HHS maintains, enforces, imposes, or continues in effect any packaging requirement for liquid nicotine containers, including a child-resistant packaging requirement.

summary.headline: A 2016 law requires liquid nicotine containers sold or imported into the United States to use child-resistant packaging that meets federal safety standards.
summary.what_it_does: The law says any liquid nicotine container sold, offered for sale, made for sale, shipped in commerce, or imported must use special packaging that is hard for children under five to open or get harmful contents from. That packaging must meet Consumer Product Safety Commission standards and testing procedures, and the requirement is treated as a standard under the Poison Prevention Packaging Act of 1970. The law excludes sealed, disposable nicotine cartridges that fit directly into electronic cigarettes if the nicotine cannot be reached through normal or foreseeable handling. It also requires the Department of Health and Human Services to consult with the Consumer Product Safety Commission on any packaging rules it sets for liquid nicotine.

who_it_affects.group: Manufacturers and importers of liquid nicotine products
who_it_affects.how: They must package liquid nicotine containers to meet the Consumer Product Safety Commission's child-resistant packaging standards before selling or importing them.

who_it_affects.group: Retailers and sellers of liquid nicotine
who_it_affects.how: They may only sell or offer for sale liquid nicotine containers that meet the required child-resistant packaging standards.
Liquid nicotine sold in the United States is required to be harder for children under five to open or access.

who_it_affects.group: Consumers who buy e-liquid or other liquid nicotine
who_it_affects.how: Containers they buy must use child-resistant packaging, while sealed disposable cartridges that fit directly into devices are excluded if their nicotine is not reachable through normal use.
